title_en: Li Ping and Gong Nian v. Mayflower Company — dispute over personal injury compensation
keywords_en: Civil; personal injury compensation dispute; first instance; intermediate people's court; Guangdong Province; natural person; legal person; Consumer Protection Law; General Principles of Civil Law; operator's duty of safety protection; third-party tort liability; causation determination; dismissal of claims; restaurant explosion; customer casualties; third-party crime; fault liability principle; guarantee; Yuehua Company personal injury compensation dispute
full_text_en:
Li Ping and Gong Nian v. Mayflower Company — dispute over personal injury compensation

Plaintiff: Li Ping, female, 39 years old, employee of the Zhuhai Municipal Education Commission, Guangdong Province, residing at Yinhua New Village, Xiangzhou, Zhuhai.

Plaintiff: Gong Nian, male, 38 years old, husband of Plaintiff Li Ping, employee of the Zhuhai Municipal Water Resources Bureau, Guangdong Province, same address as above.

Joint Agents ad litem for the two Plaintiffs: Liu Gaiqiu and Huang Xiongzhou, lawyers from Guangdong Province.

Defendant: Guangdong Zhuhai Special Economic Zone Mayflower Catering Co., Ltd. Domicile: Bitao Garden, Xiangzhou, Zhuhai, Guangdong Province.

Legal Representative: Tang Chuyuan, Director of the Company.

Agents ad litem: Luo Xiaoji and Cao Yutong, lawyers from Guangdong Nanfang Law Firm.

Plaintiffs Li Ping and Gong Nian filed a lawsuit with the Zhuhai Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province regarding a dispute over personal injury compensation with Defendant Guangdong Zhuhai Special Economic Zone Mayflower Catering Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Mayflower Company).

Plaintiffs' Allegations: The two Plaintiffs, together with their 8-year-old son Gong Shuohao, went to dine at the Mayflower Restaurant operated by the Defendant. They were seated outside a private room by the restaurant's hostess. An explosion occurred inside that private room, causing the wall of the room to collapse, resulting in Gong Shuohao's death and Li Ping's disability. The Defendant, as a catering business open to the public, has a duty not only to provide delicious food but also to provide a pleasant and safe dining environment, ensuring the personal safety of its customers. The Defendant did not prohibit customers from bringing their own alcohol into the restaurant, and used substandard wooden partition walls in the restaurant's decoration, thereby creating potential safety hazards. It was due to the Defendant's poor management that the restaurant suffered an explosion that should not have occurred, causing personal injury and death to customers. The Defendant violated Articles 11, 41, and 42 of the *Law of the People's Republic of China on the Protection of Consumer Rights and Interests* and should bear full liability for damages. The Plaintiffs request the court to order the Defendant to: (1) compensate the Plaintiffs for medical expenses, nutrition expenses, nursing fees, transportation expenses, prosthetic installation fees, disability living allowance, future treatment expenses, disability compensation, compensation for loss of fertility, funeral expenses, death compensation, and compensation for moral damages, totaling RMB 4,030,000; and (2) bear all litigation costs in this case.

Defendant's Defense: This explosion was caused by a criminal. An unsuspecting customer brought the explosive device disguised as a gift of alcohol into the restaurant. The customer had no expectation of an explosion, and the restaurant certainly could not have foreseen it. For both the Defendant and the customers, the explosion was a pure accident. The Defendant had no subjective fault and objectively did not commit any tortious act. Moreover, the explosion killed one of the Defendant's waitstaff and severely damaged the restaurant's decoration and equipment, causing direct and indirect losses of nearly RMB 1,000,000. The Defendant itself is also a victim. As a catering operator, the Defendant had fulfilled its duty to ensure the personal and property safety of the customers who came to dine. The Plaintiffs can only assert their rights against the actual wrongdoer and cannot demand compensation from the Defendant. The Plaintiffs' current lawsuit lacks factual and legal basis, and the litigation parties are not proper. Their claims should be dismissed.

Facts Found by the Zhuhai Intermediate People's Court:

At around 6:00 p.m. on October 24, 1999, Plaintiffs Li Ping and Gong Nian, together with their 8-year-old son Gong Shuohao and friends, went to dine at the Mayflower Restaurant operated by the Defendant Mayflower Company. They were seated on the second floor by the restaurant's hostess, next to a private room named "Ford." The east and south walls of the "Ford" room were brick walls, while the west and north walls were wooden partition walls. Gong Shuohao was seated on the outside of this wooden partition wall. At around 6:30 p.m., a sudden explosion occurred inside the "Ford" room. Li Ping and Gong Shuohao immediately collapsed and lost consciousness. Gong Nian, enduring his own pain, pulled away the collapsed wooden partition wall of the private room and immediately rushed Gong Shuohao to the hospital for rescue. Li Ping was also taken to the hospital. Gong Shuohao died despite rescue efforts due to traumatic asphyxia from explosive lung injuries and respiratory and circulatory failure. Li Ping suffered neurovascular injury to her left upper limb, closed abdominal injury, hemorrhagic shock, and pulmonary contusion. She underwent amputation of her left upper limb and splenectomy. After recovery, she was assessed as having a Grade 2 disability. Gong Nian sustained minor abrasions to his right outer ear and a few abrasions on his right back.

This explosion at the Mayflower Restaurant occurred when a restaurant waiter was opening the lid of a "Wuliangye Liquor" box for a customer. The explosive device disguised as a liquor box was a gift received by a doctor who was dining in the "Ford" room at the time and had been kept at home for a period. On the evening of October 24, the doctor brought this "liquor box" into the "Ford" room for dinner, and the explosion occurred when the waiter opened it. Currently, the criminal suspect who manufactured this explosive device and gave it to the doctor has been apprehended by the public security authorities and is under trial.

The above facts are confirmed by statements of both parties, witness testimony, medical diagnosis certificates, death certificates, and other evidence. After courtroom examination, the evidence can be used as the basis for determining the facts of this case.

Opinion of the Zhuhai Intermediate People's Court:

When Plaintiffs Li Ping and Gong Nian went to dine at the restaurant operated by the Defendant Mayflower Company, a consumption-service relationship was formed between them, and Mayflower Company had the obligation to ensure the personal safety of Li Ping and Gong Nian. Whether Mayflower Company fulfilled this obligation should be determined based on comprehensive factors such as the nature, characteristics, requirements, and objects of the catering industry. In this case, the personal injuries to Li Ping and Gong Nian and the death of Gong Shuohao were caused by the explosion at the Mayflower Restaurant. This explosion was the result of a third party's illegal and criminal act and had no direct causal relationship with Mayflower Company's own service conduct. Under the circumstances at that time, Mayflower Company could not foresee this explosion through reasonable care and had already fulfilled its duty to ensure customer safety.

The explosion was the necessary cause of the personal injuries to Plaintiffs Li Ping and Gong Nian and the death of Gong Shuohao. Li Ping and Gong Nian argue that the Defendant Mayflower Company's wooden partition walls did not meet standards, thereby creating potential safety hazards, and that the company should bear civil liability. The substandard wooden partition walls were only a condition, not a cause, of the injuries to Li Ping, Gong Nian, and Gong Shuohao. There is no direct causal relationship between this condition and the damage, and Mayflower Company cannot therefore bear tort liability for damages.

Article 22, paragraph 1 of the *Law of the People's Republic of China on the Protection of Consumer Rights and Interests* provides: "Business operators shall ensure that the commodities or services they provide have the quality, performance, use, and validity period they should have under normal use or receipt of services, except where the consumer knows of the defects before purchasing the commodity or receiving the service." The Defendant Mayflower Company, in addition to providing catering services, also has the right to sell tobacco and alcohol. However, according to the law, they are only obligated to guarantee the quality of the commodities they provide and have no such obligation regarding commodities brought into the restaurant by customers. This explosion was caused by a customer bringing an explosive device disguised as alcohol into the restaurant and was unrelated to the commodities or services provided by Mayflower Company. Allowing customers to bring their own alcohol into the restaurant for dining is both a customer need and a custom in the catering industry, and is not prohibited by laws, regulations, or industry rules. Mayflower Company did not prohibit customers from bringing "alcohol" into the restaurant, and its conduct was not at fault. The provisions of Articles 11, 41, and 42 of the Law on the Protection of Consumer Rights and Interests refer to the liability of business operators for causing consumer injury or death due to the provision of commodities or services. It is inappropriate for Li Ping and Gong Nian to rely on these provisions to hold Mayflower Company liable.

Under the *General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China*, tortious damage obligations are divided into general tort damages and special tort damages. Article 106, paragraph 1 of the General Principles of the Civil Law provides: "Citizens and legal persons who, through their fault, infringe upon state or collective property, or infringe upon the property or person of others, shall bear civil liability." From this provision, it can be seen that general tort damages must simultaneously satisfy four elements: objective existence of damage facts, a causal relationship between the tortious act and the damage facts, fault on the part of the actor, and the illegality of the act. None of these elements can be absent. In certain special circumstances, even if the four elements are not all present, if the law stipulates that a party shall bear civil liability, the party must bear it; this constitutes special tort damages. Special torts apply the principles of presumption of fault, no-fault liability, and equitable liability, but only when the law clearly provides for them. The tort damages lawsuit brought by Plaintiffs Li Ping and Gong Nian does not involve any other special tort damage situations provided by law. In this case, there is a clear wrongdoer, so the principle of equitable liability, which applies only when no one is at fault and must bear responsibility, cannot be applied. Therefore, only the principle of fault liability applicable to general tort damages can be applied. The Defendant Mayflower Company had fulfilled its duty of care in this explosion incident and was itself a victim of the incident. Mayflower Company had no fault in the injuries to Li Ping, Gong Nian, and Gong Shuohao, and therefore did not constitute a tort. There is also no legal interest between Mayflower Company and the wrongdoer, and it cannot substitute for the wrongdoer in bearing legal liability. Li Ping and Gong Nian should seek compensation from the third party at fault and cannot require Mayflower Company, also a victim, to bear civil liability in place of the wrongdoer. Mayflower Company's defense is well-founded and should be accepted. Article 64, paragraph 1 of the *Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China* provides: "A party has the responsibility to provide evidence in support of its own claims." Li Ping and Gong Nian claim that Mayflower Company should bear liability for compensation, but they cannot provide factual basis or legal grounds to support their claims. Therefore, their claims are not supported. Accordingly, the Zhuhai Intermediate People's Court rendered the following judgment:

Judgment:

The claims of Plaintiffs Li Ping and Gong Nian are dismissed.

Court acceptance fee of RMB 30,160 shall be jointly borne by the two Plaintiffs.

After the first-instance judgment was announced, Li Ping and Gong Nian appealed to the Guangdong High People's Court, asserting: 1. Since the first instance recognized that the appellants and the appellee Mayflower Company "formed a consumption-service relationship," this affirms that the case is a dispute over consumer rights, not a general personal injury dispute. Articles 18 and 22 of the Law on the Protection of Consumer Rights and Interests require that business operators ensure the safety of the commodities they provide and the consumption premises. By allowing customers to bring their own alcohol and by opening the bottles for customers, the appellee should have considered that the restaurant is a place for group consumption and that it was necessary to implement safety checks on items brought by customers. The appellee failed to fulfill this duty of care, leading to the occurrence of the damage in this case. 2. The appellee operated the Mayflower Restaurant without submitting the decoration for approval to the relevant authorities, violating the *Fire Protection Law of the People's Republic of China* and the *Regulations on Fire Safety Management of Public Entertainment Venues*; the west and north partition walls of the "Ford" private room did not use decoration materials with a combustion performance rating of Class A, violating the *Code for Fire Protection Design of Interior Decoration of Buildings*, and there was subjective fault regarding the occurrence of the damage in this case. The first instance stated that the restaurant used substandard wooden partition walls, creating potential safety hazards, but then deemed this only a condition, not a cause, of the injury, which is incorrect. 3. The appellee has both breached the contract and should also bear tort liability. As consumers dining at the Mayflower Restaurant without fault and suffering personal injury, the appellants should be fully compensated by the appellee, as the operator, for the damage suffered while receiving its services. The first instance disregarded consumers' rights and lacked a proper concept of protecting consumer rights and interests, thus failing to correctly apply the law and reflect necessary justice. They request that the second instance, in accordance with the Law on the Protection of Consumer Rights and Interests, reverse the judgment and order the appellee to bear liability for compensation.

The appellee Mayflower Company argued in defense: Allowing customers to bring their own alcohol into the restaurant for dining is an industry custom. The appellee had fulfilled the duty of care expected in this industry and had no fault or breach of contract regarding the damage suffered by the appellants. Both the appellants and the appellee are victims of this explosion incident. The appellants cannot conflate the appellee's service conduct with the wrongdoer's explosive act. The first-instance judgment found clear facts and correctly applied the law and should be affirmed.

Upon second-instance trial, the Guangdong High People's Court, in addition to confirming the facts found in the first instance, further found:

After the explosion in the "Ford" private room, the wooden partition walls on the west and north sides collapsed, and Li Ping and Gong Shuohao were pinned beneath them.

The appellee Mayflower Company was registered and established for business on August 31, 1998, with a business scope covering catering services and retail of domestic cigarettes and alcohol. On the application for company registration, there was an opinion "agree to apply" signed by the Fire Prevention Section of the Xiangzhou Branch of the Zhuhai Public Security Bureau. The Mayflower Restaurant has two floors with a business area greater than 100 square meters. Article 3.1.17 of the *Code for Fire Protection Design of Interior Decoration of Buildings* (National Standard GB 50222-95) stipulates: "For restaurants and scientific research laboratories that frequently use open-flame appliances, the combustion performance grade of decoration materials, except for Class A, shall be increased by one level based on the provisions of this chapter." Table 3.2.1 of the Code lists for "Entertainment and catering buildings such as dance halls and restaurants" with "business area > 100 square meters," the "combustion performance grade of decoration materials" for "walls" and "partitions" is "B1." Wall materials with a Class A combustion performance grade include marble, concrete products, glass, etc. Wall materials with a Class B1 combustion performance grade include paper-faced gypsum boards, flame-retardant molded wood composite panels, colored flame-retardant artificial boards, etc. Wall materials with a Class B2 combustion performance grade include various natural woods, etc.

Li Shikang, the person who manufactured the explosive device and disguised it as a liquor box to give to the doctor, is a farmer from Dazu County, Sichuan Province. During the trial, he indicated that he was unable to compensate for the consequences of the explosion he caused.

Opinion of the Guangdong High People's Court:

Article 122 of the *Contract Law of the People's Republic of China* provides: "If a party's breach of contract infringes upon the other party's personal or property rights, the injured party has the right to choose to demand liability for breach of contract according to this Law or to demand tort liability according to other laws." Throughout the litigation claims raised by the appellants Li Ping and Gong Nian in the first and second instances, they considered both that the appellee Mayflower Company breached the contract and that Mayflower Company committed a tort, and also believed there was a concurrence of civil liabilities, but they never made a clear choice between breach and tort. According to this legal provision, the court can only, after a full trial, handle the matter appropriately according to the principle favoring the right holder.

Regarding the issue of the appellee Mayflower Company's restaurant decoration. The appellants Li Ping and Gong Nian argue that the Mayflower Restaurant's decoration was not submitted for approval and violated fire safety management regulations, creating potential safety hazards, and thus should bear tort liability. Investigation reveals that before opening for business, Mayflower Company had already submitted to and obtained approval from the public security fire department; the claim that it was not submitted for approval is inconsistent with the facts. Furthermore, whether decoration materials comply with fire safety management regulations only reflects the materials' flame-retardant performance, not their explosion resistance. Materials with high flame-retardant performance do not necessarily have strong explosion resistance. For example, glass with a Class A flame-retardant performance has much lower explosion resistance than natural wood with a Class B2 flame-retardant performance. Moreover, Li Ping, Gong Nian, and Gong Shuohao were not burned to death or injured due to insufficient flame retardancy of the wooden partition walls. Whether using wooden boards as partition walls for restaurant private rooms complies with fire safety management regulations has no necessary causal relationship with the damage consequences in this case. There is no mandatory legal provision regarding the explosion resistance that wooden partition walls should possess, so Mayflower Company cannot be held legally liable for improper decoration on this ground.

Regarding whether the appellee Mayflower Company breached the contract. Mayflower Company accepted the appellants Li Ping, Gong Nian, and their family for dining at its restaurant, forming a contractual relationship primarily involving consumption and service. Article 60, paragraph 2 of the *Contract Law of the People's Republic of China* provides: "The parties shall follow the principle of good faith, and perform obligations of notification, assistance, and confidentiality according to the nature, purpose, and trade practices of the contract." As the operator in the consumption-service contract, Mayflower Company, in addition to fully performing the obligations expressly agreed upon in the contract, should also perform the ancillary obligation to protect consumers' personal and property rights from illegal infringement, in accordance with Article 60 of the Contract Law. To fulfill this ancillary obligation, the operator must, based on the nature, characteristics, and conditions of its industry, be constantly and cautiously attentive to protecting consumers' personal and property safety. However, due to the suddenness, concealment, and increasingly intelligent and diversified methods of criminal offenses, even if the operator gives due attention and takes precautions, it cannot completely prevent criminal offenses against customers' personal or property rights. Once such infringement occurs, whether the operator has breached the contract can only be judged by whether it exercised reasonable care and caution. It is an industry custom for the Mayflower Restaurant to accept customers bringing their own alcohol for dining. With regard to alcoholic products brought into the restaurant by customers, given the current social environment in China, it is neither necessary nor feasible to require operators to adopt security inspection measures as strict as those used for air travel. Since the outer packaging of this explosive device closely resembled real alcohol, it was difficult for an ordinary person to identify it by sight alone. The customer who brought the device had kept it at home for a period without discovering the danger. Therefore, requiring the waiter, when opening the lid of the alcohol box, to judge that danger existed is an unreasonable demand. By exercising reasonable care and caution, the Mayflower Restaurant could not have identified the explosive device disguised as alcohol, and therefore there was no breach of contract.

Regarding whether the appellee Mayflower Company committed a tort. According to the Law on the Protection of Consumer Rights and Interests, operators are responsible for the commodities or services they provide, which naturally does not include responsibility for items brought by consumers themselves. When the appellants Li Ping, Gong Nian, and their family dined at the Mayflower Restaurant, they were crushed and killed or injured by the collapsed wooden partition wall. The collapse of the wooden partition wall was caused by the explosion created by a criminal, and the responsibility naturally lies with the criminal. Mayflower Company had no common intent with the criminal to commit a tort, nor did it engage in any joint tortious act. Therefore, it cannot be found that Mayflower Company committed a tort under the Law on the Protection of Consumer Rights and Interests.

In summary, the appellee, Mayflower Company, neither breached the contract nor committed a tort in this case, and therefore cannot be held civilly liable on the grounds of breach of contract or tort. The Mayflower Company and the appellants, Li Ping and Gong Nian, both suffered misfortune in the same explosion incident. Although the wrongdoer has now been apprehended, due to his lack of financial capacity to pay compensation, both parties face the situation of being unable to obtain full compensation. In this context, it should be noted that the Mayflower Company, as a legal person enterprise, allowed customers to bring their own beverages for the purpose of profit, which led to the restaurant explosion. The restaurant's wooden partition wall could not withstand the explosion, and its collapse caused innocent harm to Li Ping, Gong Nian, and their family. Although the Mayflower Company had no legally attributable fault requiring it to bear civil liability in this explosion incident, it was not entirely unrelated to the harm suffered by Li Ping, Gong Nian, and their family. It should also be noted that while both parties were victims in the same incident, Li Ping, Gong Nian, and their family sustained damage to their survival rights while engaging in dining conduct that benefited the Mayflower Company's profitability, whereas the Mayflower Company's damage was primarily to its business interests. Comparing the two, Li Ping and Gong Nian suffered greater harm than the Mayflower Company, and all sectors of society (including the Mayflower Company itself) deeply sympathize with the plight of Li Ping, Gong Nian, and their family. Article 157 of the *Opinions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (Trial Implementation)* provides: "Where neither party is at fault for the damage, but one party is harmed in the course of activities for the benefit of the other party or for common interests, the other party or the beneficiary may be ordered to provide certain economic compensation." Based on this provision and the financial situation of Li Ping, Gong Nian, and their family, and in order to balance the resulting losses of both parties, it is appropriate, in the court's discretion, to order the Mayflower Company to provide some economic compensation to Li Ping and Gong Nian. The trial court's finding that the Mayflower Company did not constitute breach of contract or tort and therefore could not be held civilly liable was correct. However, without considering the imbalance of interests between the parties, and merely dismissing Li Ping and Gong Nian's claims on the grounds that they should seek compensation from the wrongdoer, does not comply with the provisions of Article 4 of the General Principles of the Civil Law, which states: "Civil activities shall adhere to the principles of voluntariness, fairness, equivalence for value, good faith, and creditworthiness." The judgment was improper and should be corrected. Accordingly, the Guangdong High People's Court, pursuant to Article 153, paragraph 1, item (2) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, on November 26, 2001, rendered the following judgment:

1. The civil judgment of the first instance is reversed.

2. The appellee, Mayflower Company, shall pay compensation of RMB 300,000 to the appellants, Li Ping and Gong Nian.

The total case acceptance fees for the first and second instances are RMB 60,320, to be borne equally by the two parties.
